newsitem.title: UK: Policing Internet virtually impossible - experts.
newsitem.headline: Policing Internet virtually impossible - experts.

text.p: Policing the worldwide Internet for pornographic or violent material is an almost impossible task that relies more on self-regulation by providers and users than government agencies, experts said on Thursday.

As German prosecutors brought charges against a local manager of U.S. online service CompuServe Corp in connection with child pornography on the Internet, officials acknowledged the seemingly insurmountable problems they faced in regulating the contents of cyberspace.
"It is impossible to police the Internet," said Matthew Bath, editor of Internet.H magazine.

"It is so vast. Billons and billions of dollars have been poured into it. Sixty-two million people worldwide use it. Any single person can set up a website. How do you monitor 62 million transactions a day?"
A spokesman for Britain's Department of Trade and Industry said nobody specifically polices the Internet.
"There is a voluntary code that the Internet people set up themselves with government support. It's a discreet form of self-regulation."

In Britain, information on the Internet comes under the same laws covering pornographic or dangerous material in written or video form. Local police, or special investigative units, are alerted by Internet users, servicers or regulatory groups about offensive and illegal material.
"To a great extent we rely on members to report on other members," Jonathan Bulkeley, managing director of America Online UK, one of the world's largest service providers, told Sky television news.
"We do have some responsibility and we do participate but it is impossible for us to police the content of the Internet."

Bulkeley said hundreds of times a day America Online wipes out material and closes accounts of clients providing material it finds dangerous. But because it is a public access network that anybody anywhere can use to communicate, most of the regulatory activity has to be reactive.
"Nobody can be everywhere. The wonderful thing about this medium is that it is a communication medium and it creates a global community."

Lawyers have also been studying how to police the network, which because of its lack of national boundaries makes it a regulatory nightmare. They have been trying to work out what is illegal or harmful -- always keeping in mind the freedom of speech issue.

"We do have the well-being of customers and ultimately their fundamental freedoms at heart," Janet Henderson, a lawyer and rights strategy manager for Internet sevices at British Telecommunications told a recent London conference on combating violence and pornography in cyberspace.

BT, which launched its Internet access service last March, has adopted a "taste and decency" policy. Illegal material found through its access to the computer network is reported to the Internet Watch Foundation.
The foundation, which was founded last October, will pass on information about potentially illegal material to the police.
It also wants to encourage legal material to be classified, allowing users to block access to certain subjects with filtering software.
Magazine editor Matthew Bath, for one, said he was not surprised by the German prosecution as more and more European nations move to clamp down on material on the Internet.
He predicts it will be the first of many more cases to come.
"A number of governments will be looking at it very closely," he said.
